title: Patanjali 1.1–1.16: "now, yoga"; yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings; practice and non-attachment (1 of 7)
hook: the most famous book about yoga opens with one word, and the word is now
tomorrow: Patanjali 1.2: the stilling of the mind's turnings (2 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shatpadi, the hymn that closed Dvaita and beyond: the wave belongs to the ocean, never the ocean to the wave. Two, and the space between is love. Today, a new week, and a new book.
screen: `TWO, AND THE SPACE BETWEEN IS LOVE.`

segments.voice: January, and the gym is packed. Monday, and the diet starts. The meditation app can wait until work calms down. A better time is always coming, and it's never quite this one. Then there's a short Sanskrit book about yoga that isn't about the poses. It's about the mind. You might expect it to open with a warning, or a promise, or a long list of what you need first. It opens with one word. And the word is now.
screen: `MONDAY. JANUARY. WHEN THINGS CALM DOWN.` → `A SHORT BOOK ABOUT THE MIND.` → `ITS FIRST WORD: NOW.`

segments.voice: The book is the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali. A sutra is a thread: a short line, packed tight, meant to be memorized and then unpacked by a teacher. The book strings them into four chapters. Who was Patanjali? Honestly, nobody knows much. Scholars' guesses for its date span several centuries. Tradition tells stories about him, including that he was an incarnation of the great serpent who holds up the world. The first thread, in Sanskrit, is atha yoga anushasanam. Now, the teaching of yoga. Atha, now, is a word Sanskrit books often start with. The Brahma Sutras open the same way: now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman. Traditionally the word is also considered auspicious, a good sound to begin with. The classic commentary, traditionally credited to Vyasa, says atha marks a beginning: here the teaching starts. Later teachers found more in it. Now means the preparation is over. Now means you've arrived with whatever brought you here: a restless mind, a bad week, curiosity. Now means yoga isn't something that happens after your life gets sorted out. It's the sorting. This week walks the first sixteen threads, slowly. Tomorrow, the definition of what yoga actually is. Today, just the first word.
screen: `A SUTRA IS A THREAD.` · `WHO WAS PATANJALI? NOBODY KNOWS MUCH.` · `ATHA: NOW, THE TEACHING BEGINS.` · `YOGA ISN'T AFTER YOUR LIFE. IT'S THE SORTING.` · then, large: `ATHA YOGĀNUŚĀSANAM.`

segments.voice: Sit exactly as you are, without fixing your posture or waiting for quiet, and notice what's here: the nearest sound, the feeling in your hands, the mood you brought in. Whenever your mind leaves for later or earlier, say the word gently, now, and come back; you'll probably say it many times, and every time counts as starting. If you pray, you can offer this now to God.
Atha, now. The first thread of the Yoga Sutras is atha yoga anushasanam: now, the teaching of yoga. Everything the book will teach, it teaches to someone who has already begun.
Your line: now. Not Monday, not January, not later. Day two ninety-five, and you've already begun.

howItsDone: The Yoga Sutras are studied line by line with a teacher and a commentary, often chanted in Sanskrit first; many yoga schools, in India and around the world, open their study with the first sutra.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): the review recalled the sugar line, but day 294 now closes on the Shatpadi wave-and-ocean verse; fixed. The hook opened 'Think about' and 'Now picture' and claimed 'the most famous book ever written about yoga', 'about two thousand years old' and 'shaped nearly every serious yoga teacher'; rewritten without the superlative, date and sweep. Teach: cut the sutra count and the year range, 'the oldest commentary' is now 'the classic commentary, traditionally credited to Vyasa', 'teachers have always' softened.

Dating of the Yoga Sutras: scholarly estimates range roughly from the 2nd century BCE to the 5th century CE; the script says 'from about twenty-two hundred years ago to about fifteen hundred'. Confirm.
Number of sutras: 195 or 196 depending on the recension; the script says 'about a hundred and ninety-five'.
Tradition identifies Patanjali with Adishesha (Ananta), the serpent; confirm the phrasing 'the great serpent who holds up the world'.
The Sanskrit of 1.1 is quoted in the original (public domain); transliteration spelled for listening in the voice.
